definition: To support something from below, or to serve as the basis for an idea or claim.
example: Shared trust underpins every lasting friendship, even more than common interests do.
nuance: Underpin is the opposite of undermine: one strengthens a thing from beneath, while the other weakens it from beneath.
prompt: A student explains the evidence behind her science fair conclusion.
options: Weeks of daily measurements underpin her claim that light matters most.
The serious flaws a judge discovered underpin her claim, so she has to abandon it.
She took a red marker to underpin the key results printed on her poster.
She worried the judges would underpin how many hours she had spent.
reasons: The measurements are the foundation her claim rests on, so the word fits.
Flaws that force her to drop the claim weaken it. That is undermining, not supporting.
Drawing a line beneath words is underlining. This word has nothing to do with marking a page.
This treats the word like underestimate, but it does not mean judging something too low.

practice.prompt: Builders inspect an old farmhouse whose walls have started to sag.
options: To underpin the house, the owners plan to remove its stone foundation.
The family chose to underpin the sagging house by painting its front door red.
The crew will pour fresh concrete beneath the walls to underpin them.
Deep cracks in the cellar underpin the walls, which is why the house keeps sinking.
reasons: Taking the foundation away removes support instead of adding it.
Paint changes how the house looks but does nothing to hold the structure up.
Adding solid material underneath to hold the walls up is exactly this kind of support.
Cracks that let the house sink weaken it. They do the opposite of holding it up.
